I have gathered substantial material from the sources I could reach. Here are the verse-by-verse notes.

---

## 2 Chronicles 17 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview

This chapter (unique to Chronicles; the parallel in Kings — 1 Kings 15:24; 22:41–51 — is far briefer) introduces Jehoshaphat's reign. It presents him in an entirely favourable light: personal piety, religious reform, a nationwide teaching mission, peace with surrounding nations, and military strength. Raymond Dillard notes the chapter is structured as an expansion of the general statements in vv. 1–6: fortifications (v. 2) are developed in vv. 12b–19; wealth and honour (v. 5) in vv. 10–12a; and religious devotion (vv. 3, 6) in vv. 7–9. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

---

### v. 1 — *Jehoshaphat succeeded Asa and strengthened himself against Israel.*

Jehoshaphat was about 35 years old at his accession (2 Chr 20:31; 1 Kgs 22:41–42) and reigned 25 years (c. 873–848 BC), probably including a three-year coregency with the ailing Asa. His name means "Jehovah is Judge." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

"Strengthened himself against Israel" means he fortified his defences facing the northern kingdom. Ahab was now in his fourth year and pursuing aggressive idolatry (1 Kgs 16:30–33), making the northern border a military, political and spiritual threat. Gill says Jehoshaphat did this by fortifying cities, building castles and raising a standing army. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

Mackintosh (cited at Precept Austin) warns that "Israel and Israel's king were ever a snare to the heart of Jehoshaphat," but in the freshness of his early reign he fortified against them — a pattern often seen in Christians who are most watchful against the sins that later ensnare them. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

---

### v. 2 — *He stationed troops in every fortified city of Judah and put garrisons in the land and in the Ephraimite cities Asa had captured.*

Jehoshaphat placed forces (Hebrew *ḥayil*) and garrisons (*netsibim*) in the key defensive positions. The cities of Ephraim refer to those Asa captured earlier (2 Chr 15:8). Gill notes these were soldiers stationed to protect the frontiers. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary points out that the Hebrew verb for "placed" is literally "he gave" forces, i.e., he distributed his military resources wisely. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

Mathew Henry observes that Jehoshaphat strengthened himself not by a foreign league (as his father Asa did with Syria) but "by fair and regular methods, on which he might expect the blessing of God and in which he trusted God." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

---

### v. 3 — *The LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek out the Baals.*

"Walked in the earlier ways of his father David" — Gill explains this means David's best, early ways, before the sins involving Uriah and Bathsheba and the census numbering. The Targum renders "the Word of the Lord was for his help." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Septuagint omits "David," making the reference purely to Asa — "he walked in the first ways of his father." But even if "David" is original, the sense is that he followed the faithful part of David's pattern, not his later failings. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

Trapp (cited by Guzik) says: "In the first ways, which David walked in before he fell into those horrid sins of murder and adultery." Spurgeon added, "Have you never noticed the career of David? What a happy life David's was up to one point!… But that hour when he… saw Bathsheba… put an end to the happy days of David." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

Matthew Henry draws the practical lesson: "Many good people have had their first ways, which were their best ways, their first love, which was their strongest love; and in every copy we propose to write after, we must single out that only which is good, and that chiefly which is best." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

"Baalim" (plural) refers to the various local manifestations of Baal worship — Baal-berith, Baal-zebub, Baal-peor — depending on the place of worship. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

---

### v. 4 — *He sought the God of his father and walked by His commandments rather than the practices of Israel.*

He sought (Hebrew *darash*) the LORD exclusively — in prayer, worship and enquiry. "The practices of Israel" refers particularly to the northern kingdom's systematic idolatry centred on the golden calves at Dan and Bethel. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that "the doings of Israel" marks the northern kingdom as the more typical and systematic example of wrong — idolatry "by a law" with the calves and images. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

Guzik notes that the Chronicler constantly contrasts Judah's and Israel's paths for his post-exilic readers: "Your destiny, as an individual and as a nation, can either be like that of Judah or Israel." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

---

### v. 5 — *So the LORD established the kingdom in his hand, and all Judah brought him tribute, so that he had an abundance of riches and honour.*

"Piety is the best prop of government," writes Gill; "the throne is best supported and established by truth, righteousness, and mercy." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The "presents" (Hebrew *minḥah*) were voluntary gifts from the people, though customary at a king's accession (cf. 1 Sam 10:27). Guzik links this to the principle of Matt 6:33 and Ps 37:4 — because Jehoshaphat sought God first, God exalted him. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

**Denominational note:** The connection drawn here between piety and material blessing ("riches and honour") is handled differently across traditions. Reformed and conservative evangelical teachers (Gill, Henry, Guzik) see this as a specific covenant fulfilment under Deuteronomy 28 — God rewarding fidelity in the terms of the Old Covenant. Pentecostal and charismatic traditions (Enduring Word comes from this stable) tend to draw more direct parallels to NT believers. The text is typically not used in prosperity-gospel teaching on the approved sites, though the pattern of "seek God → receive blessing" could be co-opted. The approved sources surveyed here all maintain that the Chronicler's point is the covenant faithfulness of God, not a mechanical prosperity formula.

---

### v. 6 — *His heart took delight in the ways of the LORD; furthermore, he removed the high places and Asherah poles from Judah.*

"His heart was lifted up in the ways of the LORD" — the Hebrew verb *gābah* can carry a bad sense (pride, Ps 131:1) or a good one (exaltation, Isa 52:13). Here it means his heart was enlarged, encouraged, and took courage in godly things. Matthew Henry: "He never thought he could do enough for God. He was lively and affectionate in his religion, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord, cheerful and pleasant in it." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

**The high places problem:** 1 Kings 22:43 says Jehoshaphat did *not* remove the high places, yet 2 Chronicles 17:6 says he did. Adam Clarke (Methodist commentator, cited by Guzik) resolves this by distinguishing two kinds: (1) idolatrous high places (which Jehoshaphat removed) and (2) those consecrated to the true God before the Temple was built (which he left). Selman adds, "They may also witness to the deep hold of the Canaanite and syncretic forms of religion on ordinary Israelites." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

The Asherah poles (KJV "groves") were wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah. These had been removed by Asa but had been reintroduced in the latter, negligent part of his reign. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

Peake's Commentary notes the tension with 2 Chr 20:33 (= 1 Kgs 22:43) but does not offer resolution, simply flagging the inconsistency. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-17.html)

---

### v. 7 — *In his third year, Jehoshaphat sent his officials Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the cities of Judah.*

The Hebrew text says literally "he sent *to* his princes" (*shālaḥ*), meaning he sent orders to his princes to ensure the teaching was carried out — not necessarily that the princes themselves did all the teaching. The princes lent their civil authority to back the priests and Levites. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html) Gill explains they were sent "to see that they were taught, and oblige them to attend to the instructions… and to back with their authority the priests and Levites, whose proper work it was to instruct." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The teaching mission began in the third year of his reign — early enough to show priority but after he had first secured the kingdom militarily. This is the first time in Chronicles that an itinerant Bible-teaching team is explicitly described; previously only priests are said to teach, but here Levites are included. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

---

### v. 8 — *Accompanied by Levites — Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah — along with the priests Elishama and Jehoram.*

None of these individuals are named elsewhere. The team consisted of five princes (civil), nine Levites (trained in the law and temple service), and two priests (whose lips were to keep knowledge — Mal 2:7). Gill remarks they were "principal persons, and fit for the work they were sent about." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

Guzik quotes Knapp: "By this little band of princes, Levites and priests, sixteen in all, Jehoshaphat did more toward impressing the surrounding nations with a sense of his power than the largest and best-equipped standing army could have secured to him." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

---

### v. 9 — *They taught throughout Judah, taking with them the Book of the Law of the LORD. They went throughout the towns of Judah and taught the people.*

"They had the book of the law of the Lord with them" — Ellicott identifies this as the Pentateuch, and if this notice derives from a contemporary source (e.g., "the words of Jehu the son of Hanani," 2 Chr 20:34), it is a significant early witness to a written Torah. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/17.htm)

G. Campbell Morgan (cited by Guzik) likens this to "the holding of Special Missions throughout the cities of Judah, for the specific purpose of proclaiming and interpreting 'the book of the law of Jehovah.'" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

Adam Clarke (Methodist) drew a parallel to the Wesleyan itinerant ministry: "Such an itinerant ministry established in these kingdoms for upwards of fourscore years, teaching the pure, unadulterated doctrines of the Gospel… has been the principal means, in the hand of God, of preserving the lands from those convulsions and revolutions that have ruined and nearly dissolved the European continent." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

Trapp contrasts the effect of military deployment with the teaching mission: "It is said (v. 2) Jehoshaphat placed forces in all the fenced cities; yet it is not said thereupon that 'the fear of the Lord fell upon the neighbour nations.' But when he had established a preaching ministry in all the cities, then his enemies had a fear, and made no war." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

---

### v. 10 — *The dread of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms surrounding Judah, so that they did not make war against Jehoshaphat.*

"The fear of the LORD" (Hebrew *paḥad*) conveys a supernatural awe and dread. Gill suggests it was raised in part by neighbouring nations observing that religion was revived in Judah and correlating that with Judah's prosperity and formidability in the past. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary calls this "the moral effect of this peaceful war of Jehoshaphat." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

This fulfills Proverbs 16:7: "When a man's ways please the LORD, he makes even his enemies to be at peace with him" (cf. Gen 35:5; 1 Chr 22:9). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/17.htm)

Gaebelein's Annotated Bible calls this "a fulfillment of Deuteronomy 11:22–25." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/2-chronicles-17.html)

---

### v. 11 — *Some Philistines brought gifts and silver as tribute, and the Arabs brought him 7,700 rams and 7,700 goats.*

The Philistine tribute may have come from those around Gerar whom Asa had previously subdued and made tributary (2 Chr 14:14). The Arabs — likely the Scenite Arabs — brought flocks, fearing Jehoshaphat might otherwise seize them as his father had done (2 Chr 14:15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew word translated "tribute silver" (*massā'*) literally means "bearing" or "a load/weight," possibly meaning "silver of great weight." The significance is that both Philistines and Arabians brought their payments without attempting to slip out of their obligations. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

Dr. Constable observes: "Again we see Gentiles bringing gifts to the Davidic king who walked in the ways of the Lord, as in Solomon's day (cf. 2 Chr 9:14; 26:8)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-17.html)

---

### v. 12 — *Jehoshaphat grew stronger and stronger, and he built fortresses and store cities in Judah.*

"Castles" (KJV) is better rendered "fortresses" — Hebrew *bīrāniyyôt*, found only here and in 2 Chr 27:4, a later Hebrew term connected with *bîrâ* (palace/citadel, e.g., Ezra 6:2; Neh 1:1). "Store cities" were for stockpiling grain, wine and provisions against invasion. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

August Konkel (cited at Precept Austin) notes that archaeological excavations have confirmed extensive fortification in rural Judah during this period, including a line of highway forts in the Jordan Valley near the Dead Sea datable to Jehoshaphat's time. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

---

### v. 13 — *He kept vast supplies in the cities of Judah and had warriors in Jerusalem who were mighty men of valour.*

The Hebrew phrase translated "had much business" (*melā'kâ*) is better rendered "he had much labour/property in the cities of Judah." The Pulpit Commentary suggests the meaning is that he bestowed much pains on the cities of Judah, and had men of war in Jerusalem. Keil maintains the rendering "substance" or "property." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

---

### vv. 14–16 — *The commanders of Judah: Adnah (300,000), Jehohanan (280,000), Amasiah son of Zichri, the volunteer for the LORD (200,000).*

These three "captains of thousands" (Hebrew *śar*, "prince") were the principal officers over Judah's forces. Adnah, named first with the largest corps, was likely commander-in-chief. The Judahite total is 780,000. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/17.htm)

**Amasiah, "who willingly offered himself to the LORD"** — Gill offers two interpretations: either he volunteered to fight the LORD's battles without stipend, or (following Kimchi) he offered gold and silver to the Temple treasury. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

Spurgeon (via Guzik) draws a broad application: "There is no lawful occupation in which a man cannot thoroughly serve the Lord. It is a great privilege and blessing to be set apart to the work of winning souls; but we must never separate that work from all the rest of the callings of life, as though it alone were sacred, and all the rest were secular and almost sinful. Serve God where you are." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

---

### vv. 17–18 — *From Benjamin: Eliada (200,000 armed with bows and shields), and Jehozabad (180,000 armed for war).*

The Benjaminites were known for their skill with the bow and shield (cf. 2 Chr 14:8). Their total is 380,000. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

---

### v. 19 — *These served the king, besides those stationed in the fortified cities throughout Judah.*

"These waited on the king" (Hebrew *hameshāretîm*, "those who ministered to the king") — this enormous five-division army (total 1,160,000) was the king's standing army in Jerusalem, while separate garrisons were spread throughout Judah. Gill argues these men served in rotation, as David's forces did (1 Chr 27:1), so the numbers need not imply they were all present simultaneously. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

---

### The Question of the Army Numbers

The total — 1,160,000 fighting men from just two tribes — far exceeds David's census (Judah 500,000; 2 Sam 24:9) and Asa's army (580,000; 2 Chr 14:8). The Pulpit Commentary states bluntly: "The numbers… are not only absolutely unreliable, but in themselves impossible… the text is no doubt corrupt." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html) Ellicott likewise calls such an increase "unaccountable." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/17.htm) Peake's Commentary calls them "fabulous numbers" that "stamp the section as unhistorical so far as its details are concerned." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-17.html)

Gill, representing the older conservative approach, offers several harmonising explanations: a long period of peace had allowed population growth; many had migrated from the ten northern tribes to Judah; and the Abrahamic promise of multiplication was being fulfilled. He also argues the men served in rotation and were never all present together. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/17.htm)

The Pulpit Commentary suggests Professor Murphy's theory that the five divisions corresponded to five territorial divisions of the southern kingdom, with Adnah over Judah proper, Jehohanan over the Danite/Philistine contingent, Amasiah over Simeon and the Arabs, Eliada over Benjamin, and Jehozabad over annexed Ephraim — but concedes that "no suppositions of this kind can avail to explain the numbers in the text, which is no doubt corrupt." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-17.html)

---

### Denominational Distinctives

**Pentecostal/Charismatic:** David Guzik (Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel tradition) emphasises that Jehoshaphat's "most powerful security move was not military but spiritual" and draws direct practical applications: "True national and personal strength comes not first from military might or defenses, but from wholehearted commitment to God's Word." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** Adam Clarke's commentary is cited on the high places resolution (two kinds of high places) and on the itinerant teaching ministry. Clarke explicitly compares Jehoshaphat's teaching mission to the Wesleyan circuit riders: "Such an itinerant ministry… has been the principal means, in the hand of God, of preserving the lands." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/)

**Reformed/Puritan:** Matthew Henry devotes extended treatment to Jehoshaphat as a model king, noting his heart being "lifted up in the ways of the Lord" — meaning bold, cheerful, fervent service. Trapp (Puritan) contrasts military and spiritual means of national security. Spurgeon (Reformed Baptist) is cited for the warning about David's fall and for the application that Amasiah's "willingly offering himself to the LORD" applies to every lawful occupation. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-17/; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

**Lutheran and Anglican:** No dedicated material from lcms.org, 1517.org, or distinctively Anglican commentary was retrieved in the available searches.

---

### Other Views

**Modern Critical Scholarship:** Peake's Commentary regards the teaching mission of vv. 7–9 as historically improbable: "It is difficult to regard these statements as historical, they betray too clearly the tendency characteristic of the Chronicler." The Chronicler, writing for a post-exilic audience, is said to project his own concern for the Law back onto Jehoshaphat's reign. The army numbers are "fabulous" and "stamp the section as unhistorical." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/2-chronicles-17.html)

The Pulpit Commentary and Ellicott both acknowledge the Chronicler's theological shaping of the material while treating the core outline of Jehoshaphat's prosperity as historically grounded. Raymond Dillard (quoted at Precept Austin) notes the Chronicler's deliberate parallels between Asa and Jehoshaphat and his message that "God never fails to reward fidelity." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-17-commentary)

**Catholic and Orthodox:** No material was retrieved from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org in the available searches.
